summary: Defines a MIB module of textual conventions for commonly used pseudowire management information. Other pseudowire MIB modules can import them rather than each defining its own versions.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every form having its own way of writing the same thing, this note provides shared ones. Network management documents about pseudowires borrow them.

questions: what is a textual convention in a mib
subtitle: A shared set of MIB data types for managing pseudowires, so each pseudowire MIB does not reinvent them.

tldr.problem: Pseudowire-related MIB modules would each need to define their own representations of common management values such as identifiers and status.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5542 defines the PW-TC-STD-MIB module of textual conventions, covering identifiers and indexes, operational status, control word status, fault bits, fragmentation size and fragmentation status. Other PW MIB modules import them.
tldr.outcome: PW MIB modules can reuse one agreed definition per concept. The module defines no managed objects of its own.

today: RFC 5542 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it stands as the definition of these pseudowire textual conventions.

sections.title: What This Module Is For
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols. It holds textual conventions (TCs) used for pseudowire (PW) technology and for Pseudowire Edge-to-Edge Emulation (PWE3) MIB modules. The abstract states the intent: these TCs are to be imported and used in PW-related MIB modules that would otherwise define their own representations.

The module is named PW-TC-STD-MIB and its identity is pwTcStdMIB, registered as { mib-2 188 }. It was last updated on 21 April 2009 and has one revision, the original version.
sections.plainLanguage: Pseudowire documents keep needing the same kinds of labels. This note writes those labels down once so everyone can reuse them.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content:
Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store called the Management Information Base. Objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and defined using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This module is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580 (all STD 58). For the overall framework the RFC points to section 7 of RFC 3410.

A textual convention gives a name and a precise meaning to a basic type, so that many objects can share it. The module imports MODULE-IDENTITY, Unsigned32 and mib-2 from SNMPv2-SMI, and TEXTUAL-CONVENTION from SNMPv2-TC.
sections.plainLanguage: Network gear keeps a big notebook of facts about itself. This note defines some standard ways of writing certain facts in that notebook.

sections.title: Identifiers and Index Types
sections.content:
Several conventions are plain Unsigned32 values with a display hint of d (decimal).

  • PwGroupID: an administrative identification for grouping a set of service-specific pseudowire services.
  • PwIDType: the pseudowire identifier, used together with other fields to identify the PW in the signaling session.
  • PwIndexType: a unique value greater than zero for each locally defined PW, used to index MIB tables. Values are recommended to be assigned contiguously from 1, and the value for each PW MUST stay constant at least from one re-initialization to the next.
  • PwIndexOrZeroType: the same, but also allows zero. The meaning of zero is object-specific and must be defined by each object that uses it, for example when the PW is unknown or when none or all PWs are meant.
  • PwCfgIndexOrzero: an index into configuration tables for technology-specific information; zero means no additional configuration applies.

Two more identify attachments in generalized FEC signaling: PwAttachmentIdentifierType, an octet string of 0 to 255 octets where a NULL identifier has zero length, and PwGenIdType, a value from 0 to 254 for the Attachment Group Identifier and Attachment Individual Identifier types.
sections.plainLanguage: These are like ticket numbers. Each pseudowire gets its own number so tables can point to it, and zero can be used to mean 'none' or 'not known'.

sections.title: Status Conventions
sections.content:
PwOperStatusTC gives the operational status of a PW as an integer: up(1) ready to pass packets, down(2) signaling not finished or service-level indications say it is not passing packets, testing(3) admin status set to test, dormant(4) pending an external event, notPresent(5) a component is missing (configuration error, incomplete configuration or missing hardware), and lowerLayerDown(6) lower-layer interfaces for the underlying PSN are not up.

PwStatus is a set of bits for faults affecting the PW and its interfaces: pwNotForwarding(0), servicePwRxFault(1), servicePwTxFault(2), psnPwRxFault(3) and psnPwTxFault(4). If no bits are set, no faults are reported.
sections.plainLanguage: Like a traffic light with extra notes: working, not working yet, being tested, waiting, or missing a part. A separate set of flags says what kind of fault was seen.

sections.title: Control Word and Fragmentation Conventions
sections.content:
PwCwStatusTC reports how control word (CW) negotiation stands, based on local configuration and what the peer indicated. Its values are waitingForNextMsg(1), sentWrongBitErrorCode(2), rxWithdrawWithWrongBitErrorCode(3), illegalReceivedBit(4), cwPresent(5), cwNotPresent(6) and notYetKnown(7). It cites RFC 4447.

For fragmentation, PwFragSize is the desired fragmentation length in bytes, where zero means fragmentation is not desired for packets bound for the PSN. PwFragStatus is a bit set: noFrag(0), cfgFragGreaterThanPsnMtu(1), cfgFragButRemoteIncapable(2), remoteFragCapable(3) and fragEnabled(4). Fragmentation will be used only if the local node is configured for it, the peer can accept fragmented packets and the CW is in use. It cites RFC 4623.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ends must agree on a few options first. These labels record whether they have agreed yet, and whether big packets will be cut into smaller pieces.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The module defines no management objects, only textual conventions that other PWE3 MIB modules may use. The RFC says meaningful security considerations can only be written in the MIB modules that define management objects, so this document has no impact on the security of the Internet.

For IANA, the module uses one object identifier value recorded in the SMI Numbers registry: pwTcStdMIB is { mib-2 188 }.
sections.plainLanguage: This note only provides labels and does not control anything, so it has no security risks by itself. The documents that use the labels must handle security.

items.label: down
items.desc: Signaling not finished, or the PW is not passing packets.

items.label: testing
items.desc: AdminStatus at the PW level is set to test.

items.label: dormant
items.desc: Pending, waiting for an external event.

items.label: notPresent
items.desc: A component needed to set up the PW is missing.

items.label: lowerLayerDown
items.desc: Lower-layer interfaces for the PSN are not up.
